routes.description: Establish objective moral facts by identifying attitude-independent moral truths, eliminating leading anti-realist interpretations of ordinary moral claims, and defending intellectual appearances as prima facie grounds for realist conclusions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least some moral propositions are justified as true independently of attitudes, rival semantic accounts fail to explain the relevant discourse, and ethical intuitions can legitimately support that conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least some justified moral truths retain their validity independently of individual or collective attitudes.

centralBridges.description: Reject global error theory, stance-dependent truth conditions, and non-cognitivist treatment as adequate accounts of the relevant moral judgments.
Establish that noninferential intellectual appearances receive prima facie epistemic weight and can ground reasoning toward realism.
Identify contexts in which moral assertions have propositionally structured, truth-apt content that cannot be reduced to expressive or attitude-reporting functions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how familiar first-order judgments can support realism without requiring ordinary speakers to begin with an explicit metaethical theory.
Clarify the distinctive practical authority claimed for objective moral reasons relative to preference-dependent considerations.

routes.description: Resist the inference to objective moral facts by denying that ordinary discourse or intuitive appearances determine realist commitments, developing a contextual quietist alternative, and challenging the epistemic and metaphilosophical assumptions of the realist argument.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the realist elimination is non-exhaustive, ordinary moral language remains meaningful without determinate realist content, and intuitive appearances lack sufficient shared or theory-neutral force to establish stance-independent facts.

motionBridge.description: Show that moral practice and discourse need not commit speakers to stance-independent moral facts and do not establish realism.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that contextual, quietist, or indeterminate uses of moral language escape the realist taxonomy of anti-realist alternatives.
Show that realist appearances are disputed, interpretation-dependent, or shaped by pragmatic, cultural, linguistic, and philosophical conditions.
Account for meaningful moral communication through variable use and context without assigning uniform realist or anti-realist semantics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge attempts to infer a determinate folk metaethics from surveys or philosophically trained responses.
Explain why practical importance or motivation need not depend on stance-independent reasons or facts.

sections.title: Objective moral truth and the anti-realist alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue contains the motion-level dispute over attitude-independent truth and whether error theory, stance dependence, and non-cognitivism exhaust the alternatives to realism.

sections.title: Moral language, contextual use, and quietism
sections.rationale: The semantic clash determines whether ordinary assertions encode stable realist propositions or can remain meaningful through context-sensitive uses without determinate metaethical commitments.

sections.title: Intuition, intellectual appearances, and philosophical method
sections.rationale: Ethical intuitionism depends on the epistemic standing of pre-analytic appearances, while the opposing route challenges their interpretation, reliability, generality, and methodological role.

sections.title: Common sense, empirical evidence, and folk metaethics
sections.rationale: Claims about common sense affect the dialectical starting point, making the determinacy of ordinary commitments and the methods used to measure them materially burden-relevant.

sections.title: Normative authority, motivation, and practical significance
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether objectivity supplies distinctive authority or motivation and whether practical consequences can illuminate the difference between realist and preference-based morality.
